text:
One of the best businesses to run with GrokBot is a directory.

A directory is basically just curated data on a website. You pick a topic and you say, here are the best XYZ in this topic.

It's a good $10K, $25K, $100K a month business, 

Here's the whole setup:

1) Pick the niche. Pickleball equipment. Board games that are good for parties. Something you already have taste in.

2) Build the site on Astro. Astro specifically is really good at directories.

3) Set up a research agent. Every day it investigates a new brand and writes a great page on that brand as Markdown.

4) It hands the page to the engineer, who posts it.

5) Rinse and repeat until you're getting thousands of visits a month.

6) Then add an agent that collects referral links and does outbound to get deals.

Step 6 only works after step 5. Nobody gives you a deal when the site has no traffic.

Once the directory is getting visits, you have a foundation. 

Put a niche newsletter on a subdomain and link people over to the directory with your referral link. Those warm leads become sponsors in the newsletter.

And the whole SEO game is changing right now. People are going to ChatGPT and Google AI overviews to consume content, and platforms like that need directories. There's too much information out there, so curated is what's helpful.

Pick the niche, let it write the pages, then go get the deals

article.title: Grok Bot: Build a 1-Person Company with AI Agents
article.preview_text:
Billy Howell sends the Arlington Bagel to 6,000 Arlingtonians every Thursday.
His cousin Marshall used to research it, assemble it, edit it, and man the email desk. Marshall left for a summer camp

blocks.text: Billy Howell sends the Arlington Bagel to 6,000 Arlingtonians every Thursday.
His cousin Marshall used to research it, assemble it, edit it, and man the email desk. Marshall left for a summer camp with no internet.
The newsletter is now ran by Grok Bot agents: a chief of staff, research, sales, a Beehive specialist, a social lead, and an inbox monitor. Billy sets the direction and approves the work.
The stakes: GrokBot runs $200 to $300 a month. That is the entire payroll. The company only makes sense if the team earns it back.
Your headcount is capped, and that is the point
GrokBot gives every agent a shape, a color, and one thread. It reads like DMs with a teammate.

Most people treat AI like browser tabs. One idea, one agent, one thread they abandon by Friday. Tokens vanish, context turns to mush, and the company that was supposed to run itself becomes a second job.
Billy runs six agents on one business. Heavy use in week one still left him around 10% of his monthly allowance.

Every agent on your team shares one computer in the cloud. Add a newsletter, a Twitter account, and a Gmail receipt sorter to the same roster and you pay for that bloat three times: in tokens, in speed, and in quality.
A one-person company scales by adding judgment, not by adding agents.
Hire a chief of staff before anything else
Think of this agent as your COO.
Give it the company as it exists. Billy pointed his at Notion, Slack, and Gmail.
Then one prompt: take stock of this business, and name the top three agents we should create first to drive revenue.
The mission is revenue. The org chart follows the mission.
His chief of staff returned three roles: a research agent for newsletter items, a sales agent, and a Beehive specialist for platform questions.
The rule: if your business runs on a platform, that platform gets its own hire. Your COO stays a manager instead of an expert in everything.
Run the ball for a week
Week two is execution. New agents wait. Skills wait. Connections were the only thing Billy allowed himself to touch.
Founders starting from zero should point the team at the boring first mile: buy the domain, stand up the site, set up the Gmail, build the first prospect list.

One trap to watch: agents that shop for the perfect setup forever. Billy lost three weeks to an agent weighing Notion against local files against Google Sheets. He ended it in one message: we are doing Notion.
You make the decision. The team does the work.
Promote, then hire
This is the move that separates a company from a pile of chat threads.
Have your chief of staff do the exact job once. Review the output. Once it works, say: create an agent that does that thing you just did.
Then give the new hire a goal it can measure, like emails sent or visits earned.
The cycle: COO does it → you review it → the new agent inherits it → a routine runs it.
Week three is also when you cut. Roles that idle come off the roster.
Manage by five line brief
Routines are the scheduled jobs that move the ball while you sleep.
Billy asked his chief of staff one question: based on how we ran this week, what routines should we set up?
Now each agent files a short end of day report. Five lines: what you made, what is new, what blocks you.
His social lead builds the Instagram graphics and runs the content calendar, then reports up. The chief of staff rolls everything into one view for Billy: what shipped, what is stuck, what needs you.
Five lines is the whole design. Longer reports burn tokens and cloud the context.

Agents also message each other for updates. Billy mostly works through his chief of staff, and he skips the middleman when a job needs detail, exactly like a founder walking over to the designer's desk.
Five lines is a status report. Ten pages is a token bill.
Train the team to review like you
Billy runs adversarial QA loops in Codex and calls it a general agent pattern.
The move: once an agent finishes a work product, tell it to convene a panel of sub-agents and attack the work for three rounds.
His output arrives at roughly 90% done instead of roughly 50%.
Then make the training permanent. Give feedback on a batch of work and say: turn this thread into a skill another agent uses when it reviews.
That is an employee handbook, written once, applied forever.
The honest caveat: autonomy comes later. Billy spent days in the weeds with his team before the routines carried the load.
Where a one-person company makes money

Sales. Billy connected GrokBot to his Gmail and had it watch inbound. It surfaced an email he had missed from a local bagel shop owner. He and his wife went over the next morning, ate free bagels, and talked sponsorship.
His sales agent priced every ad slot against the market and the newsletter's growth, then built a sales sheet he could hand to a local business.
Outbound. Keep the pipeline small on purpose:
Monday: add five prospects to the list. Then: pick the top three, build a custom ad package, draft the email, hand it to the chief of staff.
Billy's claim: that beats 200 outbound emails at a time. For a local newsletter, quality closes the deal.
Automation. Once a workflow works, remove the ambiguity.
GrokBot filters roughly 200 potential news items down to the keepers. A make com automation writes the two sentence blurbs in his format, every week, identically.
His reasoning is a manager's reasoning: a high performing employee spends the week on judgment, and a script handles the formatting.
The sequence: build → execute → automate.
4 companies one person can staff this way

Newsletter. Any niche. Pick a topic where you already know the best sources. Board games, tech, sports. The source list lives in Notion, the research agent fills cards twice a week, and the issue ships Thursday through Beehive.

Shopify. Billy pays for a second GrokBot account, $200, purely to keep the context clean. Separate company, separate team: a sourcing agent, a developer agent, an email agent. It found Import Yeti on its own and pulled supplier and margin data into a report on each product idea.

Directories. Curated data on a website. A research agent writes one brand page a day in Markdown, a coding agent publishes it, a third agent collects referral links and does outbound once traffic arrives. Greg's framing: a directory is a real 10K, 25K, or 100K a month business, and AI answers make curated data more valuable.

Your own infrastructure. Cloudflare, Porkbun for domains, Astro for static sites, connected to GitHub. Billy needed a booking link and preferred to skip the subscription. He reviewed mockups from his phone on the beach, picked one, and shipped it live. Two to three hours for a stack he will use for years.
2 habits that keep a solo operator fast

Let the team work on their computer. Files that bounce between your desktop, their machine, and Notion create a scavenger hunt, and you end up working on the system instead of the product. Billy's instruction: build it on your computer, and when I have reviewed it, send it to chat and put it in Notion.

Bound every research task. His template: here are three ideas, research each one, tell me the cost, tell me the price, give me your top three recommendations. Open ended research runs for two weeks and returns nothing.
Action checklist
Pick one company. One GrokBot account, one mission, one product.
Hire a chief of staff. Feed it your existing docs and ask for the three roles that drive revenue.
Spend week two on output alone.
Fill the gaps in week three, and cut the roles that idle.
Ask your chief of staff which routines move the ball overnight, then set them.
Move the repeatable, business critical steps to a cheap automation outside the team.
Give it one month, on one project, run like a real company.
Final thoughts
The old ceiling on a solo business was hours. One person could research, write, sell, and support, and that person ran out of day.
The new ceiling is tokens and context. Both reward restraint.
Small roster. One project. Three hires to start. Five line reports. Three bounded ideas per research task.

Billy calls newsletter plus directory the lowest barrier entry point, and the two stack together. A referral link in the directory becomes a warm lead. A warm lead becomes a sponsor in the newsletter. One human approves both.
The businesses start small: $2,000 a month, then $5,000, then more if the thing has legs. Rowan started the rundown as a newsletter too.
"Set up GrokBot for one project and run it like a real team." Billy Howell
